COS 700 research · University of Pretoria

Repairing radio telescope data damaged by interference

Satellites, aircraft and phone networks drown out the faint radio sky. MeerKAT has to throw those samples away, leaving holes in what it measures. A generative AI model, a conditional diffusion network, fills the holes from the data that survived. Drag across each picture to compare the raw recording with the repaired one.

Real MeerKAT data

Held-out baselines from a real MeerKAT L-band observation. The diagonal stripes are fringes from the sky. Bright streaks are interference, including some the automatic flagger missed.

Simulated data

Here the true sky is known, so you can check the fill against it. Interference was injected into a simulated sky and the model never saw what lay underneath.

Jacques Malan · BSc (Hons) Computer Science, Department of Computer Science, University of Pretoria. Supervised by Prof. Anna Bosman, Prof. Kshitij Thorat and Prof. Marcel Atemkeng.
All panels of one example share a single colour scale, so samples the model did not touch look identical before and after. For display, the brightness and noise texture of the filled real-data channels are matched to the neighbouring channels. Real fills use the level-augmented model after masking both the flagger's flags and missed interference. Simulated fills come from the phase-1 model on held-out tiles.
MeerKAT is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory, a facility of the National Research Foundation. Computing on the ilifu cloud facility.
